english: Did you take attendance / has it been called?
usage: Polite; ask a classmate if attendance was already taken
반말, to a classmate you're friendly with
출석 체크 = 'attendance check', the everyday phrasing
아직 ('yet') when you're checking you didn't miss it
examples: 출석 불렀어요?
Did they take attendance?
Whispered to the person next to you as you slip in late
저 늦었는데 출석 불렀어요?
I'm late — did they already call roll?
저 늦었는데 ('I'm late, so…') frames the urgency of the question
A: 선생님, 저 왔어요. 출석 좀 체크해 주세요. / B: 네, 확인했어요.
A: Teacher, I'm here — please mark me present. / B: Yes, got it.
Use 체크해 주세요 to the TEACHER to be marked present; 부르다 is reading names, not recording
nuance: 출석 불렀어요? combines 출석 (出席, 'attendance') and the past of 부르다 ('to call out'), asking 'have they called the roll yet?' — exactly what a latecomer desperately needs to know. The polite -어요 form suits a classmate you don't know well; with a friend drop to 출석 불렀어?. The closest near-synonym is 출석 체크했어요? (출석 + the loan-word 체크), which is interchangeable in casual class talk. The critical direction split: 출석 불렀어요? asks a PEER whether the roll-call happened; to get the TEACHER to mark you present, say 출석 체크해 주세요 — don't say 출석 불러 주세요, because 부르다 means reading names aloud to the class, not individually noting your attendance. The English-speaker's biggest trap is 직역-ing 'take attendance' with 가지다 ('to take/hold an object'): 출석을 가져요 is nonsense in Korean. Also keep the antonym pair straight: 출석 (present) ↔ 결석 (absent).

structuredNuance.t: 출석 (出席 'attendance') + 불렀어요 (past of 부르다 'to call out'). Literally 'did they call attendance?' — the urgent question of a latecomer. Use polite -어요 with unfamiliar classmates; drop to 불렀어? with friends.
Peer-to-peer only. To ask a TEACHER to mark you present, switch to 출석 체크해 주세요 — 출석 불러 주세요 sounds like asking them to read names aloud to the class, which is not what you mean.
출석 체크했어요? (체크 = English 'check') is an interchangeable casual synonym. 출석 부르다 stresses the act of calling names; 출석 체크하다 stresses ticking off a list — same situation, slightly different mental image.
'Take attendance' tempts 가지다 (가져요), but Korean uses 부르다 ('call') or 체크하다. 출석을 가져요 is meaningless. Also keep 출석 (present) distinct from 결석 (absent) — they're antonyms, not synonyms.

mistakes: Saying 출석 가졌어요? for 'did you take attendance?'.
'Take attendance' is not 가지다 ('to hold/take an object'). Korean says 출석을 부르다 ('call the roll') or 출석 체크하다. Ask 출석 불렀어요? or 출석 체크했어요?
Saying 출석 불러 주세요 to mean 'mark me present'.
부르다 is reading names aloud to the class, not recording you individually. To be marked present, say 출석 (체크) 해 주세요 — 출석 불러 주세요 sounds like 'please call out the roll (to everyone).'
Confusing 출석 with 출근.
출석 is attendance at class/school; 출근 is 'going to work / clocking in.' Say 출석 for the classroom, not 출근.

english: I won't be coming to class today
usage: Polite; telling the teacher you can't come
반말, to a classmate, not the teacher
수업 못 듣다 ('can't take the class') variant
examples: 선생님, 저 오늘 결석할게요.
Teacher, I'll be absent today.
A heads-up message to the teacher before class starts
몸이 안 좋아서 오늘 결석할게요. 죄송합니다.
I'm not feeling well, so I'll miss today. Sorry.
Give the reason first (몸이 안 좋다), then apologize — omitting either feels abrupt
A: 오늘 왜 안 와요? / B: 일이 생겨서 결석하게 됐어요. 다음 수업에 뵐게요.
A: Why aren't you coming today? / B: Something came up, so I ended up having to miss class. See you next session.
결석하게 됐어요 frames it as circumstance, not personal choice — softer and more polite
nuance: 오늘 결석할게요 is 오늘 ('today') + 결석 (缺席, 'absence') + -할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 ending that signals your own intention as a courteous notice). It is how you tell a teacher or academy you won't attend — and register matters deeply: to the teacher you keep -할게요 and almost always add a reason and 죄송합니다, because a bare announcement can feel dismissive. The blame-deflecting variant 결석하게 됐어요 ('it came to be that I'll be absent') frames absence as circumstance rather than choice, which sounds noticeably more considerate. A plainer everyday alternative is 오늘 못 가요 ('I can't come today'). Against the casual register, 수업 빠질게요 ('I'll skip class') implies a voluntary choice and is fine with friends but loose to a teacher. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 결석 as a state: 결석이에요 ('I am an absence') with the copula does not announce a planned absence — you must use the verb 결석하다. And never translate 'skip class' as 수업 점프해요, which is meaningless in Korean.

structuredNuance.t: 오늘 결석할게요 = 오늘 + 결석 (缺席 'absence') + -할게요 (courteous announcement of one's own intention). It is the polite way to notify a teacher you won't attend. Always add a reason + 죄송합니다 to soften it; omitting them can feel rude.

존댓말 only when speaking to a teacher. To classmates you can drop to 결석할게 or 오늘 못 가. The softer 결석하게 됐어요 ('it ended up that I'll be absent') de-emphasises personal agency and is ideal when you want to sound regretful, not cavalier.

오늘 못 가요 ('I can't come') is the plainest alternative. 수업 빠질게요 ('I'll skip') is fine between classmates but sounds casual-to-careless to a teacher, since 빠지다 can hint at a voluntary skip. 결석하다 is the neutral, correct verb in all formal contexts.
'Be absent' tempts 결석이에요 (copula), but you cannot notify the teacher that way — use the verb: 결석할게요. Never translate 'skip class' as 점프하다 / 스킵하다; Korean uses 빠지다 (casual) or 결석하다 (formal).

mistakes: Saying 오늘 결석이에요 to announce you'll miss class.
The copula 이에요 states a label, not an intended action. To tell the teacher, use the verb: 오늘 결석할게요 (or 못 가요).
Translating 'skip class' as 수업 점프해요 / 스킵해요.
직역 of 'skip/jump' doesn't work. Korean uses 결석하다 (formal) or 수업 빠지다 (casual): 오늘 수업 빠질게요.
Announcing the absence with no reason or apology.
A bare 결석할게요 can sound abrupt to a teacher. Add a reason and 죄송합니다: 몸이 안 좋아서 오늘 결석할게요, 죄송합니다.

usage: Polite; ask the teacher or a classmate
Checking whether any was assigned at all
Asking the page range (어디까지 = 'up to where')
examples: 숙제가 뭐예요?
What's the homework?
Asked at the end of class or to a classmate you meet later
오늘 숙제 있어요? 있으면 뭐예요?
Is there homework today? If so, what is it?
Two-step: first check existence, then ask what it is — natural spoken sequence
A: 저 어제 결석해서 그런데요, 숙제가 뭐였어요? / B: 교과서 45쪽 문제 풀어 오는 거요.
A: I was absent yesterday — what was the homework? / B: Solve the problems on page 45 of the textbook. /
Past 뭐였어요 for homework already assigned; 풀어 오다 ('solve and bring') is a typical phrasing
nuance: 숙제가 뭐예요? is 숙제 (宿題, 'homework') + 가 (subject particle) + 뭐예요 ('what is it?'). It is the basic, universally usable ask for any assigned work, directed at the teacher or a classmate. The subject particle 가 is the correct choice here — 숙제를 뭐예요 is ungrammatical. A major register distinction separates 숙제 from 과제 (課題): 숙제 is everyday short practice work (drills, written exercises), while 과제 is a bigger, more formal assignment like an essay or project — using 숙제 for a term paper sounds childish, and 과제 for tiny daily exercises sounds stiff. A very practical variant is 숙제 어디까지예요? ('how far is the homework?'), because Korean classes typically assign by page range. If you missed a class, shift to past tense: 숙제가 뭐였어요?. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle error (숙제를 voids the grammar) and treating 숙제 as a verb: 'do homework' is 숙제하다 / 숙제를 하다, not 숙제다.

structuredNuance.t: 숙제 (宿題 'homework') + 가 (subject particle) + 뭐예요 ('what is it?'). Straightforward question for any assigned work. Practical variant: 숙제 어디까지예요? ('up to where is the homework?') because Korean teachers assign by page range. Missed a class? Shift to past: 숙제가 뭐였어요?.

Works with both teachers (polite -어요) and classmates. With a close friend drop the particle and go 반말: 숙제 뭐야? The formula 오늘 숙제 있어요? first checks whether any was even assigned, then 뭐예요 asks the content — two-step approach is very natural in speech.

숙제 = daily practice work (short exercises, drills); 과제 (課題) = bigger formal assignment (essay, project, presentation). Using 숙제 for a major report sounds childish; 과제 for a tiny drill sounds stiff. Match the word to the scale.
Particle error: 숙제를 뭐예요 is ungrammatical — use subject 가 (or drop it in quick speech). Also do NOT treat 숙제 as a verb: 'do homework' is 숙제하다 / 숙제를 하다, not 숙제다 / 숙제어요.

mistakes: Saying 숙제를 뭐예요?
With 뭐예요 ('what is…?') the noun takes the subject particle 가, not the object 를. Say 숙제가 뭐예요?, or in speech just 숙제 뭐예요?
Using 숙제 for a big essay/report.
숙제 is everyday practice work; a major paper or project is 과제. Calling a term paper 숙제 sounds childish — say 과제 for serious assignments.
Treating 숙제 like a verb (숙제다 / 숙제어요).
숙제 is a noun. 'Do homework' is 숙제하다 or 숙제를 하다. To say you finished it: 숙제 다 했어요, not 숙제했다 as a state.

examples: 숙제 언제까지예요?
When's the homework due?
Asked immediately after homework is assigned so you don't forget
이 과제 언제까지 내야 돼요?
By when do I have to hand in this assignment?
내야 돼요 ('have to submit') makes the obligation explicit; 내다 is the natural verb
A: 숙제 언제까지야? / B: 다음 주 수요일 수업 전까지.
A: When's it due? / B: Before class next Wednesday.
까지 anchors both deadline question and answer — note the same particle in both turns
nuance: 숙제 언제까지예요? is 숙제 + 언제 ('when') + 까지 ('until/by') + 예요. The particle 까지 is doing the essential work: 언제까지 = 'by when' (a deadline to meet). Without 까지, the question 숙제 언제예요? sounds like asking when homework takes place, not when it's due — 까지 is non-negotiable. For formal assignments, 마감 ('deadline', lit. 'closing') surfaces: 과제 마감 언제예요?. The hand-in verb of choice is 내다 ('to hand in'), the natural classroom word — 제출하다 (提出) is more formal and better suited to written/official contexts. The contrast between 까지 and 동안: 까지 pins a deadline ('by Monday'), while 동안 marks a duration ('for a week') — keep them distinct. 'Due' has no single Korean equivalent; you always construct it from 까지 + the submission verb.

structuredNuance.t: 숙제 + 언제 ('when') + 까지 ('by/until') + 예요. 언제까지 = 'by when' = asking for a deadline. Korean has no single word for 'due'; you build it with 까지 + a verb like 내다 ('to hand in'). 마감 ('closing deadline') is the formal-register alternative: 과제 마감 언제예요?.

Fine to ask both teachers and classmates. 까지 must stay in the question — omitting it gives 숙제 언제예요? which sounds like asking when class happens. To a teacher, 언제까지 내야 돼요? ('by when must I hand it in?') is a natural fuller form. Among friends: 숙제 언제까지야?.

까지 = deadline endpoint ('by Monday'); 동안 = duration ('for a week') — never swap them. 내다 = hand in (casual classroom speech); 제출하다 = submit (formal, written). Use 내다 when talking to classmates, 제출하다 in written notices or formal academic contexts.
Dropping 까지 turns the deadline question into a vague 'when?' For the act of submission, 내다 is more natural in casual speech than 제출하다 — 언제까지 내야 돼요? is the sentence to memorize.

mistakes: Asking 숙제 언제예요? for the deadline.
언제 alone asks 'when (does it happen)?' To ask a due date, add 까지 ('by'): 숙제 언제까지예요?
Looking for one word for 'due'.
Korean has no single 'due'. Express it with 까지 + a verb: 언제까지 내야 돼요? ('by when must I hand it in?'). Don't invent 듀하다.
Overusing 제출하다 in casual class talk.
제출하다 ('to submit') is formal/written. In everyday speech, 내다 ('to hand in') is more natural: 숙제 언제까지 내요?

usage: Polite; reporting to the teacher you're done
끝내다 ('to finish/complete') for a bigger task
I haven't done the homework yet
The honest opposite, with 아직 + 못
examples: 선생님, 숙제 다 했어요.
Teacher, I finished the homework.
Said when the teacher checks who's done; 선생님 opener signals deference
숙제 다 했는데 한 문제는 잘 모르겠어요.
I did all of it, but there's one problem I'm not sure about.
다 했는데 ('I did it all, but…') lets you flag a specific difficulty without seeming lazy
A: 숙제 다 했어? / B: 아니, 시간이 없어서 다 못 했어. 도와줄 수 있어?
A: Did you finish the homework? / B: No, I ran out of time so I couldn't finish. Can you help me?
다 못 했어 ('couldn't finish it all') sounds circumstantial, not careless; contrast with 안 했어 ('didn't do it')
nuance: 숙제 다 했어요 is 숙제 + 다 ('all/completely') + 했어요 (past of 하다). The word 다 is the completion marker — it converts 'I did homework' into 'I finished it all', making it far more natural than 완성했어요 ('completed', which sounds like finishing a painting or building). The 안/못 pair in the negative is the critical choice every learner must master: 안 했어요 = 'didn't do it (by choice / just didn't)', 못 했어요 = 'couldn't do it (tried but failed, ran out of time)'. To a teacher, 다 못 했어요 ('couldn't finish') is sympathetic; 안 했어요 ('didn't do it') sounds like you blew it off — choose deliberately. For a larger 과제, 끝냈어요 ('finished/wrapped up') sounds better than 했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is misplacing 다: it must precede the verb (다 했어요), not follow it.

structuredNuance.t: 숙제 + 다 ('all') + 했어요 (past of 하다). 다 is the completion marker; without it you're just saying you did some homework, not that you finished. For a larger assignment 끝냈어요 ('wrapped up/completed') is more fitting than 다 했어요.

Polite -어요 to the teacher; drop to 다 했어 with friends. When reporting to the teacher in class, lead with 선생님 as a respectful opener. If you didn't finish, pick your negative carefully: 못 했어요 (couldn't — sympathetic) vs. 안 했어요 (didn't — sounds like negligence).

다 했어요 = finished everyday homework (idiomatic); 완성했어요 = completed something creative/substantial (feels like finishing a sculpture — awkward for homework); 끝냈어요 = wrapped up a project (suits 과제 better). Three completion verbs, three scales.
Misplacing 다: it must come BEFORE the verb (다 했어요), not after. Also the 안/못 trap: 안 했어요 sounds intentional even when you just ran out of time — use 못 했어요 to communicate circumstance, not defiance.

mistakes: Saying 숙제 안 했어요 when you ran out of time.
안 했어요 = 'didn't do it (chose not to).' If you tried but couldn't finish, say 못 했어요 ('couldn't'): 숙제 다 못 했어요 — it sounds far less like you blew it off.
Using 완성했어요 for finishing homework.
완성하다 ('to complete') fits a painting, building, or big creation. For homework, the natural word is 다 했어요 (or 끝냈어요 for a project).
Putting 다 after the verb: 했어요 다.
다 ('all') comes before the verb: 다 했어요. 했어요 다 is unnatural word order.

english: Could you explain it once more?
usage: Polite; ask the teacher to repeat
반말, to a classmate helping you
Add 천천히 ('slowly') when you can't keep up
examples: 죄송한데, 이 부분 한 번 더 설명해 주세요.
Sorry — could you explain this part once more?
이 부분 ('this part') pinpoints exactly where you got lost; 죄송한데 softens the interruption
이해가 잘 안 돼서, 천천히 한 번 더 설명해 주실 수 있어요?
I don't quite get it — could you explain slowly once more?
이해가 안 돼서 ('because I don't understand') gives the reason, making the request more considerate
A: 설명해 드릴게요. 이해됐어요? / B: 아직 잘 모르겠어요. 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?
A: Let me explain. Did you follow? / B: I'm still not quite sure — could you say it once more?
다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요 is the more formal upgrade; note 말씀 used because A is superior
nuance: 한 번 더 설명해 주세요 is 한 번 ('one time') + 더 ('more/additionally') + 설명하다 (說明, 'to explain') + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). The favor form 주세요 is indispensable — it frames the explanation as a gift to you and is what makes this polite; bare 설명하세요 is a command ('you, explain!') and is rude to a teacher. 한 번 더 ('one more time') vs. 다시 ('again'): 한 번 더 stresses 'one additional time', 다시 stresses 'from scratch / over again' — both work in class. For maximum deference to a respected teacher, upgrade 말하다 to the humble-honorific 말씀하다: 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?. The word order trap: 'one more time' must be 한 번 더, NOT 한 더 번 or 더 한 번 — the number + counter unit must stay together. The English-speaker's other pitfall is expressing non-understanding: use 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't come to be understood'), not 이해하지 않아요 (sounds like you're REFUSING to understand).

structuredNuance.t: 한 번 ('one time') + 더 ('additionally') + 설명하다 (說明 'to explain') + 해 주세요 (favor form 'please do for me'). 주세요 converts an order into a polite request. Without it, 설명하세요 is a rude command to a teacher.

Can be used in class (to the teacher) or studying with a classmate. To a teacher, adding 죄송한데 ('sorry, but…') before, and optionally 이 부분 ('this part') to pinpoint what confused you, is considered more considerate than an unframed request. Maximum deference: 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?.

한 번 더 = 'one additional time' (stresses counting); 다시 = 'again / from the start' (stresses repetition). Both combine with 설명해 주세요 naturally. 천천히 설명해 주세요 adds the speed dimension — use it when pace is the problem, not the content itself.

Word order: 'one more time' is 한 번 더 — never 한 더 번 (counter rule: number + 번 must stay together, then 더 follows). Also 이해하지 않아요 sounds like refusing to understand; say 이해가 안 돼요 ('it isn't getting understood').

mistakes: Saying 설명하세요 to the teacher.
Bare -세요 here is a command ('explain!') and sounds bossy. Use the favor form: 한 번 더 설명해 주세요 ('please explain for me').
Word order 한 더 번 / 더 한 번.
The counter pattern is number + counter, then 더: 한 번 더. 한 더 번 is wrong; 더 한 번 sounds off in this request.
Saying 이해하지 않아요 for 'I don't understand'.
That sounds like 'I refuse to understand.' Natural Korean is 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't come to be understood') or 잘 모르겠어요.

usage: Polite; flag that you want to ask
Softer opener with -는데요, invites the teacher to respond
여쭤보다 (humble 'ask') to a teacher, very polite
examples: 선생님, 질문 있어요.
Teacher, I have a question.
Raise your hand and lead with this; the simplest, safest opener in class
질문 있는데요, 이 표현 언제 써요?
I have a question — when do you use this expression?
질문 있는데요 gently opens space; the teacher instinctively replies 네, 말씀하세요
A: 수업 끝나고 하나 여쭤봐도 돼요? / B: 그럼요, 이야기해요.
A: May I ask you something after class? / B: Of course, let's talk.
여쭤봐도 돼요 is the humble ask used ONLY when you are the one requesting of a superior
nuance: 질문 있어요 is 질문 (質問, 'question') + 있어요 ('there is / I have'). It's the clean, correct signal that you want to ask something. The softer version 질문 있는데요 adds the trailing -는데요 ('just so you know…'), which naturally invites the teacher to say '네, 말씀하세요' ('yes, go ahead') — more conversationally natural than the blunt flag. For a teacher specifically, elevate to the humble verb 여쭤보다 (the humble equivalent of 물어보다 'to ask'): 여쭤봐도 돼요? is noticeably more polished than 물어봐도 돼요?. The verb contrast is central: 물어보다 = plain 'to ask' (peer or below), 여쭤보다 = humble 'to ask (a superior)'. Two other traps: (1) 질문 가지고 있어요 is a 직역 of 'have a question' using 가지다 ('to hold'), which sounds like physically clutching a question — Korean uses 있다; (2) 질문하다 means to actively pose a question, so 질문할게요 = 'I'll ask now', while 질문 있어요 = 'I have one to ask (flagging it)'.

structuredNuance.t: 질문 (質問 'question') + 있어요 ('there is'). Literally 'there is a question' = 'I have a question.' The -는데요 softener (질문 있는데요) is preferred in speech because it leaves a natural pause for the teacher to respond. 질문하다 is the ACT of asking; 질문 있다 is having one to ask — different frames.

Works for teachers (polite -어요) and classmates (반말: 질문 있어). To a senior teacher or outside of class, upgrade to 여쭤봐도 돼요? ('may I humbly ask?') — adding '수업 끝나고' ('after class') shows you don't want to interrupt. Never use 여쭤보다 downward — it is strictly for asking up.

물어보다 = plain 'to ask' (neutral/downward); 여쭤보다 = humble 'to ask (upward)'. Using 물어봐도 돼요? to a respected teacher is not wrong but sounds less polished. 질문하다 vs 질문 있다: former is the action, latter is flagging you have one.

질문 가지고 있어요 (직역 of 'have a question' with 가지다 'to hold') sounds like physically gripping a question — use 있어요. Also, 질문해요 (from 질문하다) announces you're asking RIGHT NOW, not that you have one to ask — say 질문 있어요 to flag it first.

mistakes: Saying 질문 가지고 있어요 for 'I have a question'.
직역 of 'have' with 가지다 sounds like physically holding something. Korean uses 있다: 질문 있어요.
Using 물어봐도 돼요? to a respected teacher.
물어보다 is plain 'ask (a peer).' To a teacher, the humble 여쭤보다 is more polished: 여쭤봐도 돼요?
Confusing 질문하다 with 질문 있다.
질문하다 = the act of asking; 질문 있다 = having a question. To flag one, say 질문 있어요, not 질문해요 (which announces you're asking now).

english: Did you register for the course?
usage: Polite; ask a classmate about course registration
Did you sign up for classes?
등록 = enrollment/paying tuition, a related but different step
examples: 이번 학기 수강 신청 다 했어요?
Did you finish registering for all your courses this semester?
이번 학기 ('this semester') + 다 했어요 ('all done') — the practical everyday form
그 수업 자리 없어서 수강 신청 못 했어요.
That class was full so I couldn't register.
자리 없다 ('no seats') explains the failure; 수강 신청 전쟁 ('registration war') is a real student concept
A: 수강 신청했어? 한국어 회화 들어? / B: 신청하려고 했는데 마감됐어.
A: Did you register? Are you taking Korean conversation? / B: I tried to, but it closed.
마감됐다 ('it closed') captures the click-race reality of Korean university registration
nuance: 수강 신청했어요? is 수강 신청 (受講申請, 'course registration') + 했어요. 수강 means 'taking a class' (受講) and 신청 means 'application' (申請) — so it literally means 'application to take a class', which is THE standard term for signing up for courses at a university or academy each semester. The critical distinction that trips up English speakers: 수강 신청 = choosing and signing up for courses; 등록 (登錄) = officially enrolling and paying tuition (등록금). They are SEPARATE steps in the Korean system, not interchangeable — mixing them up reveals unfamiliarity with school procedures. Korean university 수강 신청 is notoriously competitive (sites crash, seats vanish in seconds), so 수강 신청 전쟁 ('registration war') and 자리 없어서 못 했어요 are culturally familiar complaints. 신청하다 alone needs an object to be meaningful (장학금 신청 = scholarship application; 휴학 신청 = leave of absence); by itself 신청했어요? is ambiguous. Verb form: 수강 신청하다 / 수강 신청을 하다 — never the copula 수강 신청이다.

structuredNuance.t: 수강 신청 (受講 'taking a class' + 申請 'application') = the act of signing up for specific courses each term. It names course selection, not tuition payment. Verb: 수강 신청하다 / 수강 신청을 하다 — never the copula 이다. Common cultural context: seats fill in seconds, so 수강 신청 전쟁 ('registration war') is a shared student experience.
Peer conversation among students around registration period. Polite -어요 with unfamiliar classmates; 반말 with friends. Never say 수강 신청이에요 (copula) for the action — always 신청했어요 / 신청할게요.

수강 신청 (course sign-up) vs. 등록 (enrolling/paying tuition, 登錄) — two separate administrative steps. 수업 등록했어요? is understandable but slightly off; natives say 수강 신청했어요?. 신청하다 alone is ambiguous without an object.

English 'register' covers both 수강 신청 and 등록, so learners conflate them. Use 수강 신청 for picking courses, 등록 / 등록금 for tuition payment. They are not interchangeable in Korean administrative and daily speech.

mistakes: Using 등록하다 to mean 'register for a course'.
등록 in school = enrolling/paying tuition (등록금). Picking courses is 수강 신청. Say 수강 신청했어요?, not 수업 등록했어요?
Saying 수강 신청이에요 instead of the verb.
수강 신청 is a noun that takes 하다: 수강 신청했어요 / 수강 신청을 했어요. The copula 이에요 doesn't express the action of signing up.
Treating 신청 as enough by itself.
신청 ('application') needs context/an object. For courses specifically, say 수강 신청; alone, 신청했어요? is ambiguous about what you applied for.

usage: Polite; ask the teacher or a classmate
When do we take the next test?
시험을 보다 ('to take an exam') phrasing
examples: 선생님, 중간고사 언제예요?
Teacher, when are the midterms?
중간고사 ('midterm exam') is the specific academic term; 시험 언제예요? alone would also be natural
다음 주에 시험 본다고 했는데 무슨 요일이에요?
You said we have a test next week — which day?
시험 본다고 했는데 ('you said we'd take a test') confirms the fact, then clarifies the day — natural follow-up question
A: 이번 시험 언제야? 기말이야? / B: 응, 3주 후에 기말 봐.
A: When's this test? Is it the final? / B: Yeah, we take the final in three weeks.
기말고사 shortened to 기말 in casual speech; 시험 보다 is the set collocation for a student taking an exam
nuance: 시험 언제예요? is 시험 (試驗, 'exam') + 언제 ('when') + 예요. Simple and correct. The most important collocation in the exam cluster: the verb a student uses for 'taking' an exam is 시험을 보다 (lit. 'to see an exam') or 시험을 치다 — never 시험을 하다 or 시험을 가지다. So 'we have a test next week' = 다음 주에 시험 봐요, 'I'm sitting the exam now' = 시험 보고 있어요. Key vocabulary orbiting 시험: 범위 ('exam scope'), 중간고사 (中間考査 'midterm'), 기말고사 (期末考査 'final exam'). The verb split: 시험을 보다 / 치다 is what a STUDENT does; 시험을 출제하다 ('to write/set the exam') is what the TEACHER does. A lurking near-homophone trap: 시험 (exam) vs. 실험 (實驗 'experiment') — they are very close in sound, completely different in meaning. The English-speaker pitfall is 시험을 하다 ('do a test') and 시험을 가지다 ('have a test') — both are unidiomatic; use 보다.

structuredNuance.t: 시험 (試驗 'exam/test') + 언제 + 예요. The key collocation: 시험을 보다 ('to take an exam', lit. 'to see') or 치다 — not 하다. 중간고사 = midterm; 기말고사 = final. Ask 범위 ('scope') right after to know what to study.

Neutral polite (-어요) works with both teachers and classmates. With close friends: 시험 언제야?. After the teacher mentions an exam, the natural follow-up pair is 시험 언제예요? then 범위가 어디예요? — two questions that go together every time an exam is announced.

시험을 보다 = student taking the exam; 시험을 치다 = same (slightly more colloquial, regional); 시험을 출제하다 = teacher writing the exam. Student and teacher use different verbs. 시험 vs. 실험: both sound similar but 실험 = lab experiment, completely different context.
'Do a test' tempts 시험을 하다, and 'have a test' tempts 시험을 가지다 — both unidiomatic. The correct verb for a student is 보다: 시험 봐요. Also watch the 시험/실험 near-homophone trap.

mistakes: Saying 시험을 해요 for 'take a test'.
The verb for sitting an exam is 보다 (or 치다): 시험을 봐요. 시험을 하다 is not idiomatic for taking one.
Confusing 시험 with 실험.
시험 = exam/test; 실험 = experiment. 실험 언제예요? would ask when the lab experiment is — say 시험 for a school test.
Saying 시험 출제했어요 as a student.
출제하다 ('to set questions') is what the teacher does. A student says 시험 봤어요 ('I took the test'), not 출제했어요.

english: How far does the exam cover?
usage: Polite; ask which material is on the test
Up to which lesson is the test?
몇 과까지 ('up to which lesson') for textbook units
examples: 시험 범위 3과부터 7과까지 맞아요?
Is the exam range lessons 3 to 7, right?
부터…까지 ('from…to') confirms a span; 맞아요? softly checks accuracy
교과서 어디까지 나와요? 프린트도 시험에 나와요?
How far in the textbook is covered? Are the handouts on it too?
나오다 ('to come out/appear') is the idiomatic verb for material appearing on an exam — high frequency
A: 시험 범위 어디까지야? / B: 교과서 5과까지고, 선생님 프린트도 다 나와.
A: How far does the test cover? / B: Up to lesson 5 in the textbook, and all the teacher's handouts.
나와 (from 나오다) used in both directions; 프린트 ('printed handout') is normal classroom vocab
nuance: 시험 범위가 어디까지예요? is 시험 범위 (試驗範圍, 'exam scope') + 가 + 어디까지 ('up to where') + 예요. 범위 is the standard school word for 'what's on the test'; 어디까지 uses the location-to-limit word 어디 to ask for the endpoint. To state a full span, combine 부터 ('from') and 까지 ('to'): 3과부터 7과까지. A key collocation: 시험에 나오다 (lit. 'to come out on the exam') is how Koreans say material 'appears on / is tested on' — 시험에 뭐 나와요? is the casual peer ask and deserves to be memorized alongside the formal 범위 question. Textbook units use the counter 과 (제3과 / 3과 = lesson 3), not 레슨. The English-speaker pitfall is 직역-ing 'cover' as 덮다 ('to cover with a lid') — 시험이 덮어요 is nonsense. Distinguish 범위 ('test span') from 분야 ('field/discipline'): 범위 is the exam's range, 분야 is a domain like medicine or law.

structuredNuance.t: 시험 범위 (試驗 + 範圍 'scope') + 어디까지 ('up to where') + 예요. 범위 = what's on the test. 어디까지 asks the endpoint; combine with 부터 to give a span: 3과부터 7과까지 ('from lesson 3 to lesson 7'). Key idiom to memorize: 시험에 나오다 = 'to appear on / be tested on' — 시험에 뭐 나와요? is the natural casual version of this question.

Ask this immediately after the teacher announces an exam — 시험 언제예요? and 시험 범위가 어디까지예요? are the natural two-question pair. With classmates drop to 범위 어디까지야?. The phrasing 시험에 뭐 나와요? ('what comes out?') is even more casual, fine between students.

범위 = the test's span of material; 분야 (分野) = a subject field/discipline (e.g., 의학 분야 'the medical field') — not interchangeable for an exam scope. Lesson counter: 과 (3과, 7과), not 레슨 — using 7 레슨까지 sounds foreign.

직역-ing 'cover' as 덮다 ('to cover with a lid') — 시험이 덮어요 is nonsense. Korean expresses exam coverage with 범위 + 까지 or the idiom 나오다: 시험에 나와요 ('it comes out on the test'). Another trap: 분야 is not a synonym of 범위 for tests.

mistakes: Translating 'cover' as 덮다.
덮다 means physically covering (with a lid/blanket). Exam coverage is 범위 + 까지, or use 나오다: 시험에 뭐 나와요? ('what's on the test?').
Saying 7 레슨까지 for textbook lessons.
Korean counts textbook units with 과: 7과까지 ('up to lesson 7'). 레슨 is rarely used for school chapters.
Using 분야 instead of 범위.
분야 = a field/discipline (e.g., 의학 분야 'the medical field'). The test's span is 범위. Ask 시험 범위가 어디까지예요?

usage: Polite; saying you need to go over the material
반말, talking to yourself or a friend
예습 = previewing, the opposite of 복습
I have no time to review
examples: 오늘 배운 거 복습 좀 해야겠어요.
I should review what I learned today.
오늘 배운 거 ('what I learned today') is the natural object; 좀 softens the resolve
시험 전에 복습 안 하면 다 까먹어요.
If I don't review before the test, I forget everything.
까먹다 ('to forget', colloquial) vs. neutral 잊어버리다; motivates why 복습 matters
A: 어제 배운 거 이해했어? / B: 조금 헷갈려서 집에서 복습 좀 해야겠어.
A: Did you understand what we learned yesterday? / B: I'm a bit confused so I should review at home.
헷갈리다 ('to be confused/mixed up') is the natural trigger word for deciding to review
nuance: 복습 좀 해야겠어요 is 복습 (復習, 'review of already-learned material') + 좀 (softener adding a slight hesitancy) + 해야겠어요 (-아/어야겠다 ending = 'I'd better do / I should do', expressing a self-directed resolution). The 좀 makes it conversational rather than formal. The indispensable three-way distinction among the 習 (습) words: 복습 = going over material you ALREADY learned (after class); 예습 = studying ahead BEFORE class; 연습 (練習) = drilling a skill (피아노 연습 'piano practice', 발음 연습 'pronunciation practice'). English uses 'review' loosely, so learners must pick the right Korean word. 복습 is a noun; it must combine with 하다: 복습하다 or 복습을 하다, never 복습이다. The casual spoken synonym 다시 보다 ('to look at again') can fill the same space informally but 복습하다 is the precise academic term. The English-speaker pitfall is 직역-ing 'review' as 다시 보다 (fine but informal) and missing the 예습/복습/연습 split entirely.

structuredNuance.t: 복습 (復習 — 復 'again' + 習 'study') = going over what you already learned. 해야겠어요 (from -아/어야겠다) = a self-directed resolution: 'I'd better do this.' 좀 softens it to a natural musing. 복습 needs 하다: 복습하다 / 복습을 하다.

Said to yourself or a classmate, not usually to a teacher. 복습 좀 해야겠다 (반말 / self-talk) is even more common than the polite form. Often comes right after a hard lesson or after being told you might forget without practice.

복습 = review after class (already studied); 예습 (豫習) = prepare before class (not yet taught); 연습 (練習) = skill drilling (not reviewing lessons). Three distinct 習 compounds — English collapses them all into 'review/practice/study.'

직역-ing 'review' as 다시 보다 is informal but acceptable; however, missing the 예습/복습/연습 split and using 복습 for pre-class preparation (that's 예습) or for skill drills (that's 연습) reveals a gap in academic vocabulary.

mistakes: Confusing 복습 with 예습.
복습 = reviewing what you already learned (after class); 예습 = previewing ahead (before class). Don't say 예습 when you mean to go back over today's lesson — say 복습.
Mixing up 복습 and 연습.
연습 ('practice') is drilling a skill (연습 문제 'practice problems', 발음 연습 'pronunciation practice'). Going over lessons is 복습. They're different 習 words.
Saying 복습이에요 instead of 복습하다.
복습 is a noun and needs 하다: 복습해요 / 복습을 해요. 복습이에요 just labels something as 'review,' not the act of reviewing.

english: I'm not sure / I don't get it
usage: Polite; honest 'I don't understand' to the teacher
이해가 안 되다 ('it doesn't get understood')
I don't know how to do this
어떻게 하는지 ('how to do it') for a method you're stuck on
examples: 음… 잘 모르겠어요.
Hmm… I'm not sure.
When the teacher asks and you can't answer; 음 buys a moment of thinking time
이 문제 잘 모르겠어요. 다시 한 번 봐 주세요.
I don't get this problem. Could you look at it again?
Pair 잘 모르겠어요 with a specific request — don't leave it hanging
A: 이 표현 이해됐어요? / B: 솔직히 아직 잘 모르겠어요. 예를 하나 더 들어 주실 수 있어요?
A: Did you understand this expression? / B: Honestly, I'm still not quite sure — could you give one more example?
솔직히 ('honestly') + 아직 ('still') + 잘 모르겠어요 is the full humble admission, followed immediately by a request
nuance: 잘 모르겠어요 is 잘 ('well') + 모르다 ('not know') + -겠- + -어요. Counterintuitively, this is SOFTER and more polite than plain 몰라요 ('I don't know'): the -겠- marker adds a hedging, tentative quality ('I'm afraid I don't quite know'), and 잘 ('well') signals incomplete rather than zero knowledge — together they signal genuine effort and humility, which is why teachers hear this phrase positively. By contrast, bare 몰라요 can sound curt or even dismissive ('dunno'). The -겠- here is NOT future tense; it's a softening modal, a frequent misreading. For 'I don't understand' as an ongoing state, the more precise phrasing is 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't come to be understood') — NOT 이해하지 않아요, which sounds like refusing to understand. Saying 이해할 수 없어요 ('it's impossible to understand') is too strong and implies the content is at fault, not you. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 몰라요 for all levels of uncertainty: reserve bare 몰라요 for quick factual 'I don't know' answers to peers; always use 잘 모르겠어요 with teachers.

structuredNuance.t: 잘 ('well') + 모르다 ('not know') + -겠- (softener) + -어요. Literally 'I don't know it well', but the -겠- makes it a tentative hedge: 'I'm afraid I don't quite know.' SOFTER than 몰라요, which is the blunt flat 'dunno.' The -겠- is not future tense here — it's a politeness buffer.

Use with teachers (polite -어요) whenever you don't understand — it signals effort and humility. With classmates, drop to 잘 모르겠어. Pair it with a follow-up action: 한 번 더 설명해 주세요 or 예를 들어 주세요 — admitting uncertainty without a next step feels incomplete in a class context.

몰라요 = blunt flat 'don't know' (ok for quick factual answers between peers); 잘 모르겠어요 = polite hedged 'not quite sure' (classroom default); 이해가 안 돼요 = 'it's not getting understood' (ongoing state, strong sense that the content hasn't clicked). 이해하지 않아요 sounds like deliberate refusal — avoid it.

Defaulting to 몰라요 for all uncertainty sounds blunt to teachers. Also: 이해할 수 없어요 ('it's impossible to understand') over-blames the content — use 이해가 안 돼요 or 잘 모르겠어요 to frame the difficulty as yours, not the material's fault.

mistakes: Saying flat 몰라요 to the teacher.
몰라요 ('dunno') can sound curt. The softer, humbler 잘 모르겠어요 ('I'm not quite sure') is the polite classroom version.
Saying 이해하지 않아요 for 'I don't understand'.
That implies you refuse to understand. Use 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't get understood') or 잘 모르겠어요.
Reading -겠- in 모르겠어요 as future.
Here -겠- softens the statement, not future tense. 잘 모르겠어요 means 'I'm not sure (right now),' not 'I will not know.'

usage: Polite; said to the teacher leaving class
다음 주 ('next week') if class is weekly
Thanks for the class / good work
Said to the teacher at the end of class
examples: 선생님, 오늘 감사했습니다. 다음 시간에 봬요!
Teacher, thank you for today. See you next class!
감사했습니다 first, then the goodbye — the natural end-of-class sequence
수고하셨습니다! 다음 주에 뵙겠습니다.
You worked hard! See you next week.
뵙겠습니다 is the most formal 'I will see you' — adds -겠- for extra deference
A: 오늘 정말 재미있었어요. 다음 시간에 봬요. / B: 그래요, 다음 주에 봬요!
A: Today was really fun. See you next class. / B: Yes, see you next week!
Both use 봬요 because they're talking to each other (equal or near-equal), confirming the humble form is not reserved for the teacher alone
nuance: 다음 시간에 봬요 is 다음 시간 ('next time/period', where 시간 means the class period) + 에 ('at/in') + 봬요 (contraction of 뵈어요, the humble form of 보다 'to see', used when encountering a SUPERIOR). The key: to a teacher you do NOT use plain 봐요 ('I see') — you use the humble 봬요 / 뵈어요 from the verb 뵈다/뵙다, which is 보다 elevated for meeting someone above you. The spelling 봬요 vs. 뵈요 confuses even native Koreans: the correct contracted form of 뵈어요 is 봬요. At the very end of class, the expected phrase to the teacher is 수고하셨습니다 ('you've worked hard'), a courtesy for someone who did effort/labour — however, 수고하셨습니다 from a student to a clearly senior teacher can feel slightly evaluative (as if you're grading their effort), so 감사합니다 is often safer and warmer. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 너를 봐요 ('I'll see you' with an explicit object pronoun and plain verb) — Korean drops the object, and the verb must be humble: just 다음 시간에 봬요. The extra-deferential 뵙겠습니다 adds future -겠- for maximum formality.

structuredNuance.t: 다음 시간 ('next class period') + 에 + 봬요 (contraction of 뵈어요, humble 'see'). Literally 'at the next period, (I humbly) see [you].' The object is dropped — you don't say 선생님을; just 다음 시간에 봬요. Spelling note: 봬요 (correct contraction of 뵈어요), NOT 뵈요.

Said at the end of class as you leave. To the teacher: 봬요 (humble) or 뵙겠습니다 (most formal). To classmates: 다음 시간에 보자 (반말) or 봬요 (polite, still fine). Pair with 감사합니다 or 수고하셨습니다 — saying goodbye alone without acknowledgment feels abrupt.

봬요 / 뵈어요 = humble 'see' (for a superior); 봐요 = plain 'see' (peers/juniors). 수고하셨습니다 = acknowledges the other person's effort (safe for peers, slightly delicate to a very senior teacher — 감사합니다 is safer). 뵙겠습니다 = most formal, adds future -겠-.

Using plain 봐요 to the teacher (understandable but less respectful). Adding an explicit object: 선생님을 봐요 sounds like a factual observation, not a farewell. The set phrase drops the object: just 다음 시간에 봬요. Also don't confuse 봬요 (humble goodbye) with 봐요 (plain see).

mistakes: Saying 다음 시간에 봐요 to the teacher.
봐요 is plain 'see.' To a teacher use the humble 봬요 / 뵈어요 (from 뵈다, 'to see a superior'): 다음 시간에 봬요.
Adding an object: 선생님을 봐요.
The goodbye drops the object. Just say 다음 시간에 봬요, not 선생님을 봐요 (which sounds like reporting that you see the teacher).
Saying 수고하셨습니다 to a much-senior teacher.
From a student to a clearly senior teacher, 수고하셨습니다 can feel evaluative. 감사합니다 ('thank you') is safer; use 수고하셨습니다 with peers/juniors.

english: Can I get a refund (on the tuition)?
usage: Polite-neutral; ask the academy about getting money back
Asking the rules before you commit
수강료 ('tuition fee') + 환불받다 ('to receive a refund')
examples: 수업 못 들을 것 같은데 환불돼요?
I don't think I can attend — can I get a refund?
State the reason (못 들을 것 같다 = 'seems like I won't be able to attend') before the ask — polite framing
한 번도 안 나갔는데 전액 환불돼요?
I never attended even once — can I get a full refund?
전액 ('full amount') clarifies you want everything back, not a partial refund
A: 중간에 그만두면 환불받을 수 있어요? / B: 네, 환불 규정에 따라 부분 환불 가능해요.
A: If I quit partway through, can I get a refund? / B: Yes, partial refunds are possible according to our refund policy.
환불받을 수 있어요 (customer's perspective, 받다) vs. 환불해 드릴게요 (academy's perspective, 하다)
nuance: 환불돼요? is 환불 (還拂, 'refund') + 되다 ('to be possible / to happen') in polite question form: 'is a refund possible?' The 되다 frames it as checking feasibility — exactly right when you're uncertain about policy. Korea has legally mandated 학원 refund schedules (you generally get more back the earlier you cancel), so asking 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? is both smart and culturally normal. The direction split is essential: 환불하다 is what the ACADEMY does (they issue the refund), while 환불받다 is what YOU do (you receive it). As a customer, 환불받고 싶어요 is correct; 환불하고 싶어요 sounds as if you intend to give a refund. Once confirmed possible, request with 환불해 주세요 ('please refund me') or 환불받고 싶어요. The English-speaker pitfall is this 하다/받다 direction confusion, plus 직역-ing 'get my money back' as 돈 다시 가져가요, which is unidiomatic. Also, 환불 (refund) vs. 할인 (discount) — these are frequently confused: 환불돼요? asks for money back, 할인돼요? asks for a price cut.

structuredNuance.t: 환불 (還拂 'refund') + 되다 ('to be possible'). Checks whether a refund is administratively possible. Korea legally regulates 학원 refund schedules, so this is a practical, commonly needed question. To request: 환불해 주세요 (asking the academy to act) or 환불받고 싶어요 (stating your desire as the recipient).

Spoken to an academy front desk or via message. Polite -어요 form is standard in this service context. Add the reason upfront (수업 못 들을 것 같아서) to sound considerate, not demanding. 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? before committing is the smart pre-enrollment question.

Direction split: 환불하다 = the academy issues the refund (their action); 환불받다 = you receive it (your action). As the customer: use 환불받다. 환불 vs. 할인: 환불 = money back (already paid); 할인 = discount (lower price upfront). Completely different transactions.
하다/받다 confusion: 환불하고 싶어요 sounds like you'll issue a refund yourself. Use 환불받고 싶어요. Also, 돈 다시 가져가요 is unidiomatic — say 환불돼요? or 환불받을 수 있어요?.

mistakes: Saying 환불하고 싶어요 as the customer.
환불하다 (issue a refund) is what the academy does. You RECEIVE one: 환불받고 싶어요 ('I'd like to get a refund').
직역-ing 'get my money back' as 돈 다시 가져가요.
That's unidiomatic. Use 환불: 환불돼요? ('can I get a refund?') or 환불받을 수 있어요?
Confusing 환불 with 할인.
환불 = a refund (money back on something paid). 할인 = a discount (lower price). Asking 할인돼요? requests a price cut, not your money back.

english: Can I get a make-up class?
usage: Polite; ask the academy for a make-up session
Can I make up what I missed?
If I'm absent, is there a make-up?
examples: 지난주에 결석했는데 보강 가능해요?
I was absent last week — can I get a make-up class?
State the missed class first, then ask; giving context is polite and practical
이번 주 못 와서요, 보강 신청하고 싶어요.
I can't come this week, so I'd like to request a make-up.
보강 신청하다 ('to apply for a make-up') is the full action form
A: 선생님, 보강은 언제 가능한지 여쭤봐도 돼요? / B: 수요일 오후에 자리 있어요.
A: Teacher, may I ask when a make-up is possible? / B: There's a spot on Wednesday afternoon.
여쭤보다 (humble 'ask') is appropriate directed at the teacher; 자리 있다 = 'there's a spot/opening'
nuance: 보강 가능해요? is 보강 (補講, 'supplementary/make-up lecture') + 가능하다 ('to be possible') in polite question form. 보강 is the precise academy term for a class session held to compensate for one you missed (or one the teacher had to reschedule). English 'make-up class' is vague; Korean's 보강 is exact. The action forms: 보강하다 / 보강을 하다 = to hold or have a make-up; 보강 신청하다 = to apply for one; 보강을 받다 = to receive/take one. The contrast set: 보강 = compensating for a MISSED session; 복습 = self-review of material you already have; 추가 수업 = a bonus class beyond the regular schedule. Don't confuse them. An important near-synonym: 보충 수업 (補充授業) is common in school settings and nearly synonymous; academies (학원) tend to use 보강. The English-speaker's famous false-friend trap: 'makeup class' as 화장 수업 — 화장 means cosmetics makeup. The correct word is 보강, full stop. Grammatically, 가능하다 takes 이/가 or no particle — 보강을 가능해요 is ungrammatical.

structuredNuance.t: 보강 (補 'supplement' + 講 'lecture') = a class session that compensates for one missed. 가능하다 = 'to be possible.' Checks whether the academy offers make-ups at all. Action forms: 보강 신청하다 (apply for one), 보강을 받다 (receive one), 보강하다 (take/hold one).

Spoken or messaged to academy staff or the teacher. Polite -어요 is standard. To the teacher use 여쭤봐도 돼요? before asking. Always state the missed class date to show you're keeping track and being responsible, not just looking for extra sessions.

보강 = making up a missed session; 복습 = self-review; 추가 수업 = extra bonus class beyond the schedule. 보충 수업 is near-synonymous, more common in school (학교) settings; 보강 is the 학원 (academy) term. Grammatically: 보강(이) 가능해요 — not 보강을 가능해요.
False friend: 화장 수업 (makeup class = cosmetics class!). The correct word is 보강. Also 보강을 가능해요 is ungrammatical — use 보강 가능해요? or 보강이 가능해요?.

mistakes: Saying 화장 수업 for 'make-up class'.
False friend! 화장 = cosmetics makeup. A make-up (supplementary) class is 보강. Ask 보강 가능해요?, never 화장 수업.
Using 추가 수업 to mean making up an absence.
추가 수업 = an extra/bonus class beyond schedule. Making up a MISSED class is 보강. Say 보강 가능해요? for what you missed.
Saying 보강을 가능해요.
가능하다 takes 이/가 or no particle: 보강(이) 가능해요. 보강을 가능해요 is ungrammatical — drop 을 or use 보강할 수 있어요.

english: How far did the class get?
usage: Polite; ask how far the class progressed
저 빠진 동안 진도 많이 나갔어요?
Did the class move a lot while I was out?
빠진 동안 ('while I was absent') for catching up
examples: 저 어제 못 와서요, 진도 어디까지 나갔어요?
I couldn't come yesterday — how far did you get?
State the absence first; 못 와서요 ('because I couldn't come') sets the context naturally
다른 반은 진도가 더 빨라요. 우리는 5과까지 나갔어요.
The other class moves faster. We got up to lesson 5.
진도가 빠르다/느리다 ('progress is fast/slow') is the idiomatic way to compare class pacing
A: 진도 어디까지 나갔어? / B: 4과 끝내고 5과 들어갔어.
A: How far did the class get? / B: We finished lesson 4 and started lesson 5.
나가다 in the question mirrors 들어가다 ('to enter, start') in the answer — natural lesson-progress vocabulary
nuance: 진도 어디까지 나갔어요? is 진도 (進度, 'curriculum progress') + 어디까지 ('up to where') + 나갔어요 (past of 나가다 'to go out/advance'). This is the standard ask when you've missed a session and need to catch up. The crucial collocation: 진도가 나가다 (lit. 'progress goes forward/out') is how Korean expresses a class MOVING through the syllabus — 나가다 (motion verb) is the set partner for 진도, and swapping it for 가다 (진도 갔어요) sounds off. Related expressions from the same set: 진도가 빠르다 ('the class is moving fast'), 진도가 느리다 ('the class is slow'), 진도를 따라가다 ('to keep up with the class pace'). The contrast: 진도 ('how far into the syllabus') vs. 범위 ('exam scope') vs. 복습 ('self-review') — 진도 is about curriculum momentum, not testing or study. The English-speaker pitfall is 직역-ing 'how far did we go' as 우리 얼마나 멀리 갔어요?, which sounds like physical distance. Use the set phrase 진도 어디까지 나갔어요?.

structuredNuance.t: 진도 (進度 'curriculum progress') + 어디까지 ('up to where') + 나갔어요 (past of 나가다). The motion verb 나가다 ('go forward/out') is the set collocation for 진도 — it captures the idea of material ADVANCING through the syllabus. Related idioms: 진도가 빠르다 ('class is moving fast'), 진도를 따라가다 ('to keep up with the pace').

Said to a classmate after an absence. 못 와서요 ('because I couldn't come') as a lead-in is considerate. With a classmate who's your friend, drop to 진도 어디까지 나갔어?. A lighter alternative for the same situation: 오늘 어디 했어요? ('what part did you do today?') — simpler but slightly less precise.

진도 = forward curriculum progress; 범위 = exam scope; 복습 = self-review. All three circle the same classroom context but mean different things. To catch up after an absence you ask 진도; to study for an exam you ask 범위; to go over what you learned you do 복습.

직역-ing 'how far did we go' as 우리 얼마나 멀리 갔어요? implies physical distance traveled — awkward or confusing in school contexts. The set phrase is 진도 어디까지 나갔어요?. Also 진도 갔어요 is off; the verb must be 나가다, not 가다.

mistakes: 직역-ing as 우리 얼마나 멀리 갔어요?
That sounds like physical distance traveled. Class progress uses 진도 + 나가다: 진도 어디까지 나갔어요?
Saying 진도 갔어요 instead of 나갔어요.
The set collocation is 진도가 나가다 ('progress advances'). 진도 갔어요 sounds off; say 진도 (많이) 나갔어요.
Confusing 진도 with 범위.
진도 = how far the class has gotten through the curriculum; 범위 = what's on the exam. To catch up after an absence, ask 진도 어디까지 나갔어요?, not 범위.

english: How did the test go? / Did you do well?
usage: Polite; ask a classmate how their exam went
망치다 ('to ruin') — when it went badly
When do the results come out?
examples: A: 시험 잘 봤어요? / B: 아니요, 좀 망친 것 같아요. 한 파트가 너무 어려웠어요.
A: Did the test go well? / B: Not really — I think I blew part of it. One section was really hard.
망친 것 같아요 ('seems like I ruined it') is more natural and modest than 나빴어요 ('it was bad')
점수 잘 나왔어요? 저는 84점 받았어요.
Did you get a good score? I got 84.
점수 나오다 ('a score comes out') + 점 받다 ('to get points') — two essential score collocations
저는 못 봤어요. 한 문제 다 틀렸어요.
I didn't do well. I got a whole question wrong.
못 봤어요 (couldn't do well) + 틀리다 ('to be wrong') for wrong answers — not 잘못하다
nuance: 시험 잘 봤어요? is 시험 + 잘 ('well') + 봤어요 (past of 보다). It reuses the key exam collocation 시험을 보다 ('to take an exam'), now in the past to ask how the exam WENT — so literally 'did you see the exam well?', meaning 'did it go well / did you do well?'. This is the natural conversational follow-up after an exam, and it reinforces the rule: the verb for taking an exam is 보다, NOT 하다. The closest near-synonym expression is 시험 어땠어요? ('how was the test?') — more open-ended, inviting a fuller answer beyond just good/bad; 잘 봤어요? presupposes you're checking on success, while 어땠어요? is a neutral open invite. Good result: 잘 봤어요 ('I did well'), 점수 잘 나왔어요 ('I got a good score'), 90점 받았어요 ('I got 90'). Bad result: 망쳤어요 (망치다 = 'to ruin/botch' — THE everyday verb for bombing; far more idiomatic than 나빴어요 'it was bad'), 못 봤어요 ('didn't do well'). Score vocabulary: 점수 (點數, 'score'), 점 (the counter for points — 90점), 점수가 나오다 / 점수를 받다. Wrong answers: 틀리다 ('to be wrong, to err') for a mistaken answer — NOT 잘못하다 ('to behave wrongly/misbehave'). The English-speaker pitfall is 시험 잘 했어요? (하다 instead of 보다) — the verb for an exam is fixed as 보다.

structuredNuance.t: 시험 + 잘 + 봤어요 (past of 보다). Literally 'did you see the exam well?' = 'did it go well?' Reinforces the key collocation: the student's verb for an exam is 보다, never 하다. Score vocabulary: 점수 (點數), 점 (points counter), 점수가 나오다 / 점수를 받다. Wrong answers: 틀리다, not 잘못하다.

Asked right after an exam, peer-to-peer. Polite -어요 with less familiar classmates; 시험 잘 봤어? with close friends. When answering badly, 망쳤어요 or 못 봤어요 are the natural honest forms — 나빴어요 ('it was bad') is technically correct but rarely used for exam results.

시험 어땠어요? = neutral open ask ('how was the test?') — the named near-synonym; 잘 봤어요? presupposes a success/failure frame and expects a yes/no-ish answer. 시험 결과 언제 나와요? = asking when graded results will be announced — different timeframe, don't conflate. 틀리다 = wrong answer (neutral); 잘못하다 = behave wrongly/make a moral mistake — completely different contexts.
'Do well' tempts 잘 했어요 (하다), but the set verb for exams is 보다: 시험 잘 봤어요?. 시험 잘 했어요? sounds slightly unnatural to a native ear. Also: 잘못하다 is not the word for a wrong exam answer — 틀리다 is.

mistakes: Saying 시험 잘 했어요? for 'did you do well?'.
The verb for an exam is 보다, not 하다. The idiomatic ask is 시험 잘 봤어요? — 시험 했어요 sounds off.
Saying 시험이 나빴어요 for 'I did badly'.
직역 of 'bad' is unnatural here. Koreans say 시험 망쳤어요 ('I bombed it', from 망치다) or 시험 못 봤어요 ('didn't do well').
Using 잘못했어요 for wrong test answers.
잘못하다 = to misbehave / do wrong (an act). A wrong answer is 틀리다: 두 문제 틀렸어요 ('I got two wrong'), not 잘못했어요.

english: Could you lend me your notes?
usage: Can you lend me your notes?
Polite; ask a classmate for their notes
Can you show me your notes?
Can I take a photo (of it)?
사진 찍다 ('take a photo') of someone's notes
examples: 미안한데, 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요?
Sorry, could you lend me your notes?
미안한데 ('sorry, but…') softens the favor request before it — essential for this kind of ask
어제 결석해서요, 필기한 거 사진 찍어도 돼요?
I was absent yesterday — can I photo your notes?
사진 찍어도 돼요? is a lower-imposition alternative to borrowing; add 돌려줄게요 if you take the actual notebook
A: 오늘 수업 노트 빌려줄 수 있어? 내가 오늘 늦게 와서 처음 부분을 못 썼어. / B: 그래, 오늘 안에 돌려줘.
A: Can you lend me today's class notes? I came late and missed the first part. / B: Sure — return it today.
돌려주다 ('to return/give back') in the reply shows the lender is already thinking about getting it back — reassure proactively
nuance: 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요? is 노트 (from English 'notes/notebook') + 좀 (softener) + 빌려주다 ('to lend') + ㄹ 수 있어요? ('can you?'). The borrow/lend distinction is the central vocabulary challenge: 빌리다 = 'to BORROW' (the action goes toward you — you take it), 빌려주다 = 'to LEND' (the action goes toward the other person — they give it to you). When asking a classmate to hand over their notes, you frame it as their lending: 빌려줄 수 있어요? ('can you lend?'). You can also say 빌릴 수 있어요? ('can I borrow?') — both are correct, but the favor-framing 빌려주다 is slightly warmer. The related word 필기 (筆記, 'written notes / what was written down during class') is the more precise term for the actual content on the page — 필기 보여줄 수 있어요? ('can you show me your notes?'). In practice, Koreans often photograph notes rather than borrow the notebook, so 사진 찍어도 돼요? is a very common, low-imposition alternative. Add 돌려줄게요 ('I'll give it back') proactively — it reassures and is considered polite. English-speaker trap: 주다 ('give') without 빌려 implies you keep it; 빌려주다 signals a loan.

structuredNuance.t: 노트 + 좀 + 빌려주다 ('to lend') + ㄹ 수 있어요? The borrow/lend split: 빌리다 = I take (borrow); 빌려주다 = they give (lend). When asking a classmate, frame it from their side with 빌려줄 수 있어요? — or equivalently 빌릴 수 있어요? from your side. Favor framing (빌려주다) is slightly warmer. 필기 = the written content; 노트 = the physical notebook.

Peer-to-peer. 미안한데 or 죄송한데 as a preface is strongly expected for favors like this. In practice, photographing notes (사진 찍어도 돼요?) is common and lower-effort than borrowing the notebook — mention 돌려줄게요 if you do take the actual book.

빌리다 = borrow (take from); 빌려주다 = lend (give to) — never use them in reverse. 노트 줄 수 있어요? ('can you give me your notes?') implies keeping it, not borrowing. 필기 is the content written; 노트 is the physical object. 노트 vs. 노트북: 노트 = notes/notebook for writing; 노트북 = laptop.

Using 주다 alone (노트 줄 수 있어요?) implies permanent transfer, not a loan. You need 빌려주다 to signal you'll return it. The 빌리다/빌려주다 direction split is the core confusion — know which person the action is directed at.

mistakes: Mixing up 빌리다 and 빌려주다.
빌리다 = you borrow (take); 빌려주다 = they lend (give). To ask a classmate to give you their notes, say 빌려줄 수 있어요? ('can you lend?') — or 빌릴 수 있어요? ('can I borrow?'), but never use them backwards.
Saying 노트 줄 수 있어요? when you'll give it back.
주다 ('give') implies keeping it. To borrow and return, use 빌려주다 ('lend'): 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요?
Confusing 노트 (notebook/notes) with 노트북.
노트 = notes/notebook for writing; 노트북 = a laptop computer. Asking 노트북 빌려줄 수 있어요? requests a laptop, not class notes.
